title: Module 3: State of the World (SOW)
content: Mastering persistence and state in AMPS.
Understanding the SOW Database.
Querying and Atomic Subscriptions.
speakerNotes: Welcome to Module 3. Today we're diving into the 'State of the World' or SOW, which is one of AMPS' most powerful features.

title: What is the SOW? 🗄️
content: SOW = State of the World.
A high-performance database within AMPS.
Stores the 'last value' for every unique message.
Enables applications to query current state immediately.
speakerNotes: Think of the SOW as a real-time database. While pub/sub handles the stream, the SOW handles the state.

title: SOW vs. Pub/Sub 🔄
content: **Pub/Sub**: Ephemeral. You get messages only while you are connected.
**SOW**: Persistent. You can ask 'What is the current price of IBM?' at any time.
Use Pub/Sub for notifications; use SOW for state management.
speakerNotes: Pub/sub is like a radio broadcast. SOW is like a library where you can look up the latest edition of a book.

title: SOW as a Last-Value Cache ⚡
content: Automatically updates existing records when a new message with the same key arrives.
Extremely low latency for both updates and queries.
Ideal for view servers and real-time dashboards.
speakerNotes: In AMPS, every time a message is published to a SOW topic, AMPS checks if that record already exists. If it does, it updates it. If not, it creates it.

title: SOW as a Document Store 📄
content: Store full JSON or XML documents.
Query based on any field within the document.
No need for fixed schemas - it's flexible like a NoSQL store.
speakerNotes: AMPS doesn't just store simple key-value pairs. It can store complex, nested documents and let you query them using XPath or SQL-92 filters.

title: SOW Keys: The Identity of a Message 🔑
content: Every SOW record must have a unique identifier called a **SOW Key**.
This key determines which record is updated during a publish.
AMPS uses this key to perform efficient lookups.
speakerNotes: The SOW Key is the 'Primary Key' of your SOW topic. It's how AMPS knows that message A and message B are updates to the same object.

title: SOW Key Strategies 🧠
content: **Content-based**: AMPS calculates the key from one or more fields (e.g., `/orderId`).
**User-provided**: The publisher explicitly provides a key in the message header.
Most applications prefer content-based keys for simplicity.
speakerNotes: With content-based keys, the publisher just sends data, and AMPS handles the identity. User-provided keys are useful when the identity isn't in the payload itself.

title: Visualizing SOW Key Calculation
content: How AMPS processes an incoming message to find its SOW record.
mermaid:
graph LR
  A[Incoming Message] --> B[Extract Key Field: /id]
  B --> C[Compute Hash]
  C --> D[SOW Key: 0x8660...]
  D --> E{Record Exists?}
  E -- Yes --> F[Update Record]
  E -- No --> G[Insert New Record]
speakerNotes: This diagram shows the flow. AMPS extracts the field, hashes it to create a SOW Key, and then decides whether to update or insert.

title: Configuring a SOW Topic 🛠️
content: <SOW>
<Topic>
<Name>Orders</Name>
<MessageType>json</MessageType>
<Key>/orderId</Key>
<FileName>./sow/%n.sow</FileName>
</Topic>
</SOW>
speakerNotes: This is a basic configuration. We name the topic, specify the format, define the key field, and provide a file path for persistence.

title: Key Configuration Fields 📝
content: **Topic**: The name of the SOW table.
**MessageType**: JSON, FIX, NVFIX, etc.
**Key**: The field(s) used to identify records.
**FileName**: Enables disk persistence (survives restarts).
speakerNotes: Notice the %n in the FileName - this is a macro that AMPS replaces with the topic name. Using FileName is critical if you want your data to be there after a server restart.

title: Querying the SOW: The 'sow' Command 🔍
content: Retrieves a point-in-time snapshot.
Returns all records matching the topic and filter.
The command completes once the results are sent.
speakerNotes: Using the 'sow' command is like running a SELECT statement in SQL. You get the current data and the connection stays open, but the query is finished.

title: Filtering SOW Queries 🧪
content: **SQL-92**: `/price > 100 AND /symbol = 'AAPL'`
**Regular Expressions**: `/symbol LIKE '(?i)ibm'`
**XPath**: `/orders/item[1]/id = 50`
speakerNotes: AMPS filters are incredibly fast because AMPS builds internal indexes to speed up matching against the SOW.

title: Atomic Query and Subscribe ⚡
content: **Problem**: If you query then subscribe, you might miss messages that happen in between.
**Solution**: AMPS provides a single command to do both atomically.
Ensures no duplicates and no gaps.
speakerNotes: This is a classic distributed systems problem. AMPS solves it by handling the registration and the snapshot in a single step on the server.

title: The 'sow_and_subscribe' Solution ✅
content: 1. AMPS registers the subscription first.
2. AMPS then runs the SOW query.
3. Client receives the snapshot, followed by real-time updates.
speakerNotes: To the application, this looks like one continuous stream of data starting with the current state.

title: Atomic Flow Diagram
content: Eliminating race conditions with sow_and_subscribe.
mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as AMPS Server
  C->>S: sow_and_subscribe
  Note over S: 1. Register Sub
  S->>C: 2. Snapshot (Record 1)
  S->>C: 2. Snapshot (Record 2)
  Note right of S: Update Arrives
  S->>C: 3. Real-time Update (Record 1 Updated)
speakerNotes: Watch how the update is delivered immediately after the snapshot records, guaranteeing consistency.

title: Module Summary 🏁
content: SOW provides last-value state and document storage.
Identity is managed via SOW Keys (Content or User).
Use `sow` for snapshots and `sow_and_subscribe` for real-time state.
Persistence is enabled via `FileName` in config.
speakerNotes: That wraps up Module 3. You now know how to manage state in AMPS. Next, we'll look at how to use these features in your code!
